Heretofore
hēr´tŏŏ-fōr´
adv. (before this time; formerly; up to now)
English here + tofore (before), a compound long naturalized in legal and biblical English. It marks a line between a past manner of things and a change now come.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Heretofore is the KJV's word for the way things have been until now, spoken most often at the moment they stop being so. Moses pleads it as a disqualification: “I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant” (Exo 4:10). Israel is warned by it at the Jordan: “come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way heretofore” (Jos 3:4). Boaz commends Ruth for coming “unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore” (Rut 2:11). And Paul uses it as a warning to the unrepentant: “I write to them which heretofore have sinned… that, if I come again, I will not spare” (2Co 13:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines heretofore as in times before the present; formerly; and notes it refers to time past as distinguished from the present.

expand to see more

HERETOFORE, adv. In times before the present; formerly.

TOFORE, adv. Before; obsolete except in composition.

FORMERLY, adv. In time past, of longer or shorter duration; heretofore.

Key Scripture

Exo 4:10 — "And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue."

Jos 3:4 — "Yet there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way heretofore."

Rut 2:11 — "And Boaz answered and said unto her, It hath fully been shewed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband: and how thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity, and art come unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore."

2Co 13:2 — "I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare:"

Modern Corruption

Joshua 3 tells Israel to follow the ark because they had not passed that way heretofore, and it is the standing pattern for guidance.

expand to see more

The instruction at the Jordan is one of the plainest statements in Scripture about how God leads. There shall be a space between you and the ark, about two thousand cubits, that ye may know the way by which ye must go — for ye have not passed this way heretofore. Israel is to keep its distance, keep its eyes on the ark, and walk into a country no living Israelite had crossed. Guidance here is not an inward impression or an inference from experience; experience is precisely what is unavailable. It is following the visible token of God's presence, at a reverent distance, into unfamiliar ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's past is not his map. Moses answers the burning bush with his history — I am not eloquent, neither heretofore — and God answers with a question about who made the mouth. The reflex is common and looks like humility: I have never been able to do this, therefore God cannot be calling me to it. Exodus 4 treats it as unbelief, and Exodus 4:14 records that the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses over it. The word heretofore describes what God is about to change.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tmol shilshom, literally yesterday and the day before — the idiom the KJV renders heretofore; Greek proamartano (G4258), to have sinned before.

expand to see more

Hebrew tmol shilshom — yesterday and third day, i.e. formerly; Exodus 4:10, Joshua 3:4.

Hebrew ethmol (H865) — yesterday, before; Ruth 2:11, 2 Samuel 15:20.

Greek proamartano (G4258) — to sin beforehand; 2 Corinthians 12:21, 13:2 only.

Hebrew aron (H727) — ark; Joshua 3:3, 3:4.

Hebrew rachaq (H7368) — to be far, keep distance; Joshua 3:4, Proverbs 22:5.

Usage

"“Ye have not passed this way heretofore” — the reason to follow the ark."

"“I am not eloquent, neither heretofore” — Moses' history offered as a refusal."

"“Them which heretofore have sinned” — Paul's warning to Corinth."
